title: Inquest hears that Stochmal's hog-tying not taught by RCMP
article: Shortly before his sudden death, Michael Stochmal's hands and feet were bound and tied together behind his back in a restraint that is rarely used by police officers, a coroner's jury heard Saturday.

The procedure -- known as hog-tying -- is not taught to city police officers, but they are not prohibited from using it, said Regina Police Service Staff Sgt. Murray Roe, a specialist in the use- of-force model used by police. Roe said he concluded the restraint was a reasonable choice given the circumstances

The inquest into Stochmal's death has heard that six police officers had difficulty subduing the "frenzied" man after he fatally stabbed his nine-year-old son in Regina the night of Sept. 1, 2001. Stochmal, who had been handcuffed and pepper-sprayed, was lying on his stomach when officers also cuffed his feet and linked that restraint to his handcuffs.

Stochmal died of apparent sudden cardiac arrest a short time later, after being lifted into the back of a nearby police cruiser. A forensic pathologist earlier told the inquest that the death was likely caused by excited delirium, which can be seen in people experiencing a psychotic episode.

Asked whether the method of restraint used was appropriate when there is evidence it can hamper a suspect's ability to breath, Roe testified: "In this particular case, I believe it was." He added that it was the officers' duty to get Stochmal under control.
Six jurors are scrutinizing the 35-year-old's death in hopes of preventing a similar future tragedy. The last of more than 20 witnesses, who were each questioned by four lawyers, testified Saturday.
Roe told the inquest the hog-tie method is not taught to police, and is used "extremely seldomly". Some evidence links the position to the threat of "positional asphyxiation (suffocation)."
"The idea is to discourage this use rather than reinforce this use," Roe said.

The sometimes testy courtroom exchange was punctuated by frequent objections as Pauline Duncan, the lawyer representing Stochmal's parents, questioned why police would allow officers to use the hog- tie method but not train them how to do it.
"The worry I have is if you do that (teach the hog-tie), you will see it used more," Roe said.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Sandy Ervin, another specialist in use-of-force models used by police, told the inquest he felt the hog-tie was a controversial method but still an appropriate use of force in the Stochmal situation. RCMP were directed to abandon use of that restraint in 2002 due to the safety concerns.

Both officers told the inquest the only other available restraint police could have used on Stochmal that night was a neck restraint - - which renders a suspect temporarily unconscious -- and both said they consider that method a higher level of force.

Ervin and Roe also each testified that use of a weapon commonly called a tazer or stun gun might have helped subdue Stochmal. RCMP officers currently use tazers, which immobilize a suspect with an electrical shock. Regina police are testing that type of weapon but the practice has not yet been adopted.
The jury will get instructions from coroner Hugh Harradance later this week, after which members may make recommendations. The jury is not allowed to assess blame.
